newsitem.title: FRANCE: French confidence drop temporary - economists.
newsitem.headline: French confidence drop temporary - economists.

text.p: A modest drop last month in French consumer confidence shown by figures released on Thursday was likely to be temporary, economists said, citing an overall improved economic outlook.
"Most likely, the March drop in consumer sentiment does not herald the start of a new deterioration," Jean-Francois Mercier of Salomon Brothers said in a research note.
"It's just temporary as overall economic conditions are improving," Morgan Stanley's Eric Chaney said in an interview.
National statistics institute INSEE released seasonally adjusted figures showing consumer confidence, on a rising trend since last autumn, fell back slightly in March.
INSEE's confidence indicator, which shows how much negative views outweigh positive ones in percentage points, slipped to -32 from -30.
The figure was still above the -38 low the index reached in December 1995 when the country was wracked by labour unrest, but well below its 10-year average of around minus 24.

Some economists say, however, the index appears to have been of little use of late in predicting consumer behaviour. They say it might have become more a reflection of consumer unhappiness than an indicator of spending plans.
One economist noted the INSEE survey contrasted sharply with other household findings pointing to a strong improvement in confidence.

An index published by independent economic association Societal and polling company BVA, found confidence rose strongly in February. Over the last two months, that survey found confidence had returned close to levels experienced between 1991 and 1993.

Economists said renewed pessimism about the labour market, likely sparked by publicity over job cuts announced by French carmaker Renault, was a key factor behind the March drop in confidence in the INSEE index. "All the noise surrounding Renault I think played a role," said Chaney.

But they said improving business sentiment should boost job growth in coming quarters. They added that while fiscal policy was expected to remain restrictive, the government was unlikely to impose new individual taxes or substantial cuts in welfare benefits during the rest of the year with the approach of the 1998 parliamentary elections.
Real private income, which grew just 0.2 percent in 1996, is expected to grow by 1.5 to 2.0 percent this year, which should bolster confidence, one economist added.

But Mercier said that with consumer confidence at relatively subdued levels, private consumption would not contribute to an expected pickup in economic growth this year. "Expansion will have to rely on exports, the end of destocking and a moderate rebound in business investment," said Mercier.
